name: Sergipe
summary_text: Sergipe stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted on a 14-1 vote; joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full equal rights from 2015; and a person may change their name and gender marker without surgery, hormones or a diagnosis under the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018. A trans visitor's documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in matters of marriage and adoption.  On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. Brazilian courts have applied that provision to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing. An expatriate legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide.  No third-gender option exists in national identity documents. Civil registries have nevertheless been able to record 'non-binary/unspecified' entries since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of the registry to a neutral gender, established as precedent for lower courts.  The statutory text does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International's country report of 12 March 2026 records that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, trans people above all, and that the legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The same report notes that gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.  Enforcement also varies geographically. The April 2026 law-firm guide reports that major cities including São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. Sergipe's smaller municipalities fall on the less-resourced side of that division.  Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. LGBTI status is recognised by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. A judge fixes the place of deprivation of liberty in a reasoned decision after consulting the person, setting out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and asking trans, travesti and intersex people which they prefer, and within it whether the general population or a specific wing or cell. The preference is recorded, later changes of placement are possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in one large state's metropolitan prison system, finding that travestis and trans women are held in units operated as masculine, some in so-called neutral or security units, and characterising placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. Protection machinery has widened in parallel: analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women.

name: Tocantins
summary_text: Tocantins has no LGBTI statute of its own in this inventory; the state stands entirely under Brazil's national framework, which applies identically in Palmas and in any other Brazilian jurisdiction. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted 14–1, and joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full equal rights from 2015.  Name and gender-marker change at the civil registry has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018 and proceeds on self-determination. Brazil has no third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry entries marked non-binary or unspecified have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of registry entries to a neutral gender as precedent.  On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held, in ADO 26 and MI 4733, that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitutes a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment of one to five years and fines. The April 2026 law-firm guide confirms that homophobia and transphobia are covered on the same footing, and that these national provisions, not any Tocantins statute, supply the criminal protection a trans visitor would rely on.  Entry and family matters follow the national rules: an expatriate legal guide updated in April 2026 records that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at the border.  The protective text does not describe routine experience. OutRight International's report of 12 March 2026 states that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, while its legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The April 2026 law-firm guide records that enforcement is uneven in practice, contrasting major urban centres, broadly welcoming and served by established legal infrastructure, against smaller cities and rural areas, where identical legal rights may still meet more social friction.
